options.label: A succession of images, scenes, ideas, emotions, and sensations that occur involuntarily in the mind during sleep
options.feedback: Correct. That is exactly what a dream is—a flow of mental content that happens on its own during certain stages of sleep.

options.label: A deliberate story the brain invents while awake to pass the time
options.feedback: Dreams happen during sleep, not while awake, and they are not deliberately invented. They are involuntary.

options.label: A physical movement of the eyes that always comes with sleep
options.feedback: That describes rapid eye movement (REM), not a dream itself. Dreams are the mental experience, not the eye motion.

options.label: A memory of a real event that replays exactly as it happened
options.feedback: Dreams are not exact replays of real events. They blend and distort content, and they occur during sleep, not as a memory of waking life.

items.ok_line: A dream is a succession of images, scenes, ideas, emotions, and sensations that happen involuntarily during sleep.
items.ko_line: A dream is not something deliberate, awake, or an exact replay—it is involuntary mental content during sleep.
items.exp_text: A dream is a chain of mental experiences—images, dynamic scenes, situations, ideas, emotions, and sensations—that arise on their own during sleep. It is not something the person chooses to make, and it is tied to certain stages of sleep, most often the rapid-eye movement stage.

items.prompt: During which sleep stage do dreams most commonly occur?

options.label: The stage just after falling asleep, called light sleep
options.feedback: Light sleep is the start of sleep, but dreams are not most common there. They mainly happen in rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep.

options.label: The deepest stage of sleep, when brain waves are very slow
options.feedback: Deep sleep has slow, synchronised brain waves, and it is not the main stage for dreaming. REM sleep is the main one.

options.label: The rapid-eye movement (REM) stage of sleep
options.feedback: Correct. During REM sleep, brain activity is high and resembles being awake, and that is the stage where most dreams occur.

options.label: All stages of sleep equally
options.feedback: Dreams are not spread equally across all stages. They occur predominantly in REM sleep, though some happen during non-REM sleep as well.

items.ok_line: Dreams occur mainly during rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep.
items.ko_line: It is REM sleep, not light sleep, deep sleep, or every stage equally.
items.exp_text: Most dreams take place in the rapid-eye movement (REM) stage of sleep. In REM, the brain is highly active, its activity resembling that of being awake, which is why vivid dreaming is so common there. Non-REM sleep can also contain dreams, but less frequently.

items.prompt: How long does the average dream last?

options.label: A few seconds, like a snapshot
options.feedback: A dream is not just a quick flash. Each dream typically lasts between 5 and 20 minutes.

options.label: Around 5 to 20 minutes
options.feedback: Correct. Each individual dream lasts roughly 5 to 20 minutes, and over a night a person dreams for more than two hours in total.

options.label: About 30 to 60 minutes
options.feedback: That is longer than typical. A single dream usually lasts only 5 to 20 minutes.

options.label: The entire night without interruption
options.feedback: Dreams do not last the whole night. They come in episodes, each one around 5 to 20 minutes long.

items.ok_line: Each dream lasts around 5 to 20 minutes.
items.ko_line: It is about 5 to 20 minutes per dream, not a few seconds, an hour, or the whole night.
items.exp_text: A single dream lasts roughly 5 to 20 minutes. Over an entire night, humans spend more than two hours dreaming altogether, since several dreams occur in sequence during sleep.

items.prompt: What is the most common emotion people experience in their dreams?

options.label: Joy
options.feedback: Joy is one of the emotions found in dreams, but it is not the most frequent. Anxiety tops the list.

options.label: Fear
options.feedback: Fear appears in dreams, but it is not the most common one. Anxiety, which is a feeling of worry or unease, is the most frequent.

options.label: Anger
options.feedback: Anger does occur in dreams, but it is not the most common emotion. Anxiety is the one reported most often.

options.label: Anxiety
options.feedback: Correct. In a large collection of dream reports, the most frequent emotion was anxiety, and negative emotions overall were more common than positive ones.

items.ok_line: Anxiety is the emotion most often felt in dreams.
items.ko_line: Joy, fear, and anger occur, but anxiety is the one reported most.
items.exp_text: Studies of thousands of dream reports show that the most common emotion in dreams is anxiety. Other emotions like anger, fear, joy, and happiness also appear, but negative feelings are generally more frequent than positive ones.

items.prompt: What kind of dreams do people who are blind from birth have?

options.label: Dreams based on other senses, like hearing and touch
options.feedback: Correct. People blind from birth do not have visual dreams; their dream content comes from senses they have, such as hearing, touch, smell, or taste.

options.label: Visual dreams just like those of sighted people
options.feedback: That is not possible for someone blind from birth, because they never had visual experience to draw on. Their dreams use other senses.

options.label: No dreams at all
options.feedback: People blind from birth do dream. They simply dream using non-visual senses like hearing and touch.

options.label: Dreams with no content at all, only feelings
options.feedback: Their dreams do have content, but it comes from senses other than sight—like touch, hearing, smell, or taste—not from nothing.

items.ok_line: People blind from birth dream with senses other than vision.
items.ko_line: Their dreams are not visual and not empty—they use other senses.
items.exp_text: A person blind from birth does not have visual dreams because they never had visual images to build them from. Instead, their dreams involve the senses they do have—hearing, touch, smell, and taste—which are present since birth.

items.prompt: How often do sexual dreams occur, according to studies of dream reports?

options.label: More than half of all dreams
options.feedback: That is far too high. Studies found sexual dreams happen no more than about 10% of the time.

options.label: No more than about 10% of the time
options.feedback: Correct. Both major studies reported that sexual content appears in at most 10% of dreams, with one finding 8% for both men and women.

options.label: Around 25% of dreams
options.feedback: That is higher than the studies found. The figure is no more than 10%, and one study found 8%.

options.label: Almost never, less than 1% of dreams
options.feedback: It is not that rare. Studies show sexual dreams occur in about 8% to 10% of dreams.

items.ok_line: Sexual dreams occur in no more than about 10% of dreams.
items.ko_line: Studies put it at 8–10%, not over half, a quarter, or under 1%.
items.exp_text: In analyses of large sets of dream reports, sexual dreams appear no more than about 10% of the time. One study reported 8% for both men and women, showing they are a minority of dream content.

items.prompt: What is the scientific study of dreams called?

options.label: Psychotherapy
options.feedback: Psychotherapy is a form of therapy that uses dream interpretation, but it is not the name of the scientific study of dreams.

options.label: Dreamwork
options.feedback: Dreamwork is a practice similar to interpretation but without seeking definite meaning. It is not the scientific field.

options.label: Oneirology
options.feedback: Correct. The scientific study of dreams is called oneirology, focusing on neurophysiology and hypotheses about dream function.

options.label: Neurophysiology
options.feedback: Neurophysiology is the study of how the nervous system works, which is part of dream research, but it is not the name for the study of dreams itself.

items.ok_line: The scientific study of dreams is oneirology.
items.ko_line: Psychotherapy, dreamwork, and neurophysiology are related, but oneirology is the correct name.
items.exp_text: Oneirology is the term for the scientific study of dreams. Modern oneirology focuses on the neurophysiology of dreaming and on testing hypotheses about what dreams do, rather than on interpreting their meanings.

items.prompt: What do ancient writings from Mesopotamia and Egypt say about dreams?

options.label: Dreams were considered meaningless random thoughts
options.feedback: On the contrary, these ancient writings treated dreams as highly meaningful, sometimes dictating what the dreamer should do afterward.

options.label: Dreams were always about predicting the weather
options.feedback: That is not what the writings say. They highlight visitation dreams, where a deity or ancestor commands actions or foretells events—not weather predictions.

options.label: Dreams came only from the dreamer's own memories
options.feedback: The ancient writings describe dreams as visitations from outside figures, not as personal recollections.

options.label: A dream figure, like a deity or ancestor, could command the dreamer to act
options.feedback: Correct. These writings describe visitation dreams, where a divine or ancestral figure tells the dreamer to do something or predicts what will happen.

items.ok_line: Ancient writings describe visitation dreams with commands from deities or ancestors.
items.ko_line: They were not random, weather-related, or memory-based—they were visitations with commands.
items.exp_text: Writings from Mesopotamia and Ancient Egypt describe visitation dreams, in which a special figure—usually a deity or a prominent ancestor—commands the dreamer to take specific actions or foretells future events. This shows that long ago dreams were thought to steer a person's behaviour after waking.

items.prompt: Why is it currently impossible to prove that animals dream?

options.label: Because a dream must be reported in words to be studied
options.feedback: Correct. To study a dream, it must be turned into a verbal report of the person's memory of it. Animals cannot give such a report, so their dreaming cannot be proven.

options.label: Because animals do not have REM sleep
options.feedback: That is not true. REM sleep is detectable in many species, and all mammals appear to experience it. The problem is the lack of verbal report.

options.label: Because animals' brains are too small to dream
options.feedback: Brain size is not the issue. The obstacle is that dreaming is only observable through verbal reports, which animals cannot provide.

options.label: Because animal dreams are always too short to detect
options.feedback: Dream length is not the reason. Even if animals dream, we have no way to get their verbal report, so we cannot confirm it.

items.ok_line: Animal dreams cannot be proven because they cannot give verbal reports.
items.ko_line: It is not about REM, brain size, or length—it is the lack of verbal report.
items.exp_text: To study a dream, it must first be turned into a verbal report—a person's account of what they remember from the dream. That report is not the dream itself, but it is the only evidence available. Since non-human animals cannot give such a report, their dreaming cannot currently be confirmed, even though many species show REM sleep.

items.prompt: What did a study of over 15,000 dream reports find about dreams after the COVID-19 pandemic began?

options.label: Dreams became shorter and less frequent
options.feedback: That was not the finding. The study found that themes about fear, illness, and death became more common, not that dreams shortened.

options.label: Dreams contained more positive emotions than before
options.feedback: The opposite was found. Negative themes like fear and death were more prevalent, not positive ones.

options.label: Themes like fear, illness, and death became two to four times more common
options.feedback: Correct. That study reported that these worrying themes were two to four times more frequent in dreams after the pandemic started.

options.label: Dreams stopped mentioning real-world events entirely
options.feedback: That is not what the study found. In fact, real-world concerns like illness and death appeared more often in dreams.

items.ok_line: Themes of fear, illness, and death became two to four times more common.
items.ko_line: It was an increase in negative themes, not shorter dreams, more positivity, or no real-world content.
items.exp_text: An analysis of more than 15,000 dream reports by Deirdre Barrett showed that after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, themes involving fear, illness, and death were two to four times more prevalent than before. This illustrates how real-world events can shape the content of dreams.
